items.prompt: Why do the front teeth (incisors) have a flat, thin edge?

options.label: To grip food without letting it slip
options.feedback: Grip comes mainly from jaw pressure and tooth position generally, not specifically from a flat edge; a flat edge is suited for a different job.

options.label: To slice through food like a small blade
options.feedback: The thin edge concentrates the bite's force into a narrow line, cutting cleanly the way a blade does.

options.label: To grind food into a paste
options.feedback: Grinding needs a broad, bumpy surface to crush food between two flat areas; a thin edge cuts rather than crushes.

options.label: To warm food before it is swallowed
options.feedback: Nothing about a tooth's shape changes food's temperature; that's not a job any tooth does.

items.ok_line: A blade shape for a cutting job.
items.ko_line: Think about what a thin, flat edge is actually shaped to do.
items.exp_title: A built-in blade at the front
items.exp_text: Incisors are shaped like small, flat chisels, with a thin edge that meets the opposing tooth precisely when the jaw closes. That edge concentrates the force of the bite into a narrow line, letting it slice cleanly through food the way a blade does rather than crushing it.

items.prompt: Why are the canine teeth pointed rather than flat?

options.label: A point spreads the bite force over a wider area
options.feedback: A point does the opposite of spreading force — it concentrates force into the smallest possible area, which is exactly why it works.

options.label: The point helps the tooth self-clean
options.feedback: Shape has no cleaning effect on a tooth; nothing about a point removes food debris.

options.label: A point makes the tooth easier to replace later
options.feedback: How a tooth is eventually replaced has nothing to do with the shape it wears while in use.

options.label: A pointed tip concentrates force so it can pierce and tear tougher food
options.feedback: The same bite force focused onto a tiny area lets a canine pierce and tear rather than merely crush.

items.ok_line: A point that pierces because the force has nowhere to spread.
items.ko_line: Ask what a narrow point does to the same amount of force compared with a flat edge.
items.exp_title: A point built to concentrate force
items.exp_text: Squeezing the jaw shut delivers the same bite force whichever tooth it passes through, but a canine's pointed tip focuses that force onto a tiny area rather than spreading it along an edge. That concentration is what lets a canine pierce and tear at tougher food, such as a stringy piece of meat, that a flatter tooth would only crush or slide across.

items.prompt: Why do molars have a broad surface covered in bumps and ridges instead of a smooth flat top?

options.label: Ridges match against ridges on the opposing tooth, trapping and crushing food between them
options.feedback: When the jaw closes, food caught between those two matching surfaces gets crushed and ground from several directions at once.

options.label: The ridges help the molar grip the gum more tightly
options.feedback: What anchors a tooth in place is its root inside the jawbone, not the pattern worn into the chewing surface.

options.label: A bumpy surface makes the tooth lighter
options.feedback: The ridges are part of the same solid enamel surface; they don't remove material or change the tooth's weight.

options.label: The bumps let food slide past more easily
options.feedback: Bumps and ridges catch and hold food between them rather than letting it slide through untouched, which is exactly what grinding needs.

items.ok_line: Ridge meets ridge, and whatever is between them gets crushed.
items.ko_line: Picture what happens to something caught between two matching bumpy surfaces pressed together.
items.exp_text: A molar's chewing surface is covered in raised cusps and grooves that are shaped to interlock with the ridges of the molar directly opposite it in the other jaw. When the jaw closes, food caught between those two matching surfaces gets crushed and ground from several directions at once, rather than simply sliced the way a flat edge would cut it.

items.prompt: Why can tooth enamel withstand years of daily chewing without wearing away?

options.label: It regrows every time it wears down
options.feedback: Enamel has no living cells within it capable of regrowing once it has formed; whatever enamel a tooth has, it keeps.

options.label: It is coated in a layer of saliva that absorbs the impact
options.feedback: Saliva keeps the mouth moist and helps protect against acid, but it forms no cushioning layer that could absorb the force of a bite.

options.label: It is built from a dense arrangement of hard mineral crystals
options.feedback: Those tightly packed crystals give enamel the structure it needs to resist repeated force and friction.

options.label: Nerves inside it stiffen the surface during chewing
options.feedback: Nerves carry sensation; they have no way to change how hard or soft the enamel surface is while chewing.

items.ok_line: Densely packed crystal, not a living material that regrows.
items.ko_line: Enamel cannot regrow or stiffen on demand; whatever protects it has to already be built into it.
items.exp_title: A structure built to resist wear, not repair itself
items.exp_text: Enamel is made almost entirely of tightly packed mineral crystals arranged in interlocking rods, giving it a hardness that lets it resist the repeated force and friction of chewing. Because those crystals are laid down once as the tooth forms and are not replaced afterward, enamel has to survive on that original structure for as long as the tooth is used.

items.prompt: Why does a cavity that reaches deep into a tooth cause pain, when the outer enamel itself has no feeling?

options.label: Deep decay releases acid that burns the gum directly
options.feedback: The pain of a deep cavity is felt in the tooth itself, at the site of decay, not from acid affecting the gum somewhere else.

options.label: It exposes nerves and blood vessels inside the tooth's core
options.feedback: Underneath the dentin lies the pulp, a soft core carrying nerves and blood vessels, and decay only hurts once it reaches that living tissue.

options.label: It makes the tooth loose in its socket, straining the jaw
options.feedback: A cavity deep enough to loosen a tooth is unusual and not what causes the sharp pain most people feel from ordinary decay; that pain has a more direct cause.

options.label: It changes the tooth's temperature
options.feedback: A cavity doesn't change a tooth's own temperature; what a deep cavity does is expose sensitive tissue that then reacts strongly to temperature from outside.

items.ok_line: The pain starts where the nerve finally gets reached.
items.ko_line: Ask what a tooth actually has, underneath enamel, that is capable of feeling anything.
items.exp_text: Enamel itself contains no nerves, which is why the earliest, most surface-level decay causes no pain at all. But underneath it lies dentin, and deeper still the pulp, a soft core carrying nerves and blood vessels, so a cavity only starts to hurt once it has eaten far enough inward to reach that living tissue.

items.prompt: Why do children lose their first set of teeth and grow a second, permanent set?

options.label: The first teeth wear out faster because they are smaller
options.feedback: Baby teeth are not lost because of wear; some remain in perfectly usable condition right up until they fall out.

options.label: Baby teeth dissolve in saliva over time
options.feedback: Saliva does not dissolve teeth; what actually happens is that the root of a baby tooth is broken down from beneath by the body itself, not by saliva.

options.label: The permanent teeth push the baby teeth out purely by growing sideways
options.feedback: The new tooth does press upward from below, but it can only do that because the old tooth's root has already been cleared out of its way, not because of sideways growth.

options.label: A growing jaw eventually has room for larger teeth, and the body clears the way for them
options.feedback: As a permanent tooth develops beneath a baby tooth, the body gradually breaks down that baby tooth's root until it falls out.

items.ok_line: Room made on purpose, for teeth that need it.
items.ko_line: Ask what has to happen to a baby tooth's root before the tooth can come loose at all.
items.exp_title: Clearing the way for something bigger
items.exp_text: A young child's jaw is too small to hold a full set of adult-sized teeth, so the first set is a temporary, smaller-scale set that fits the jaw as it is early on. As the jaw grows and a permanent tooth develops beneath a baby tooth, the body gradually breaks down that baby tooth's root until it is loose enough to fall out, making room for the larger tooth to take its place.

items.prompt: Why do wisdom teeth, the last molars to come in at the back of the jaw, often cause problems?

options.label: By the time they arrive, the jaw is often too small to fit them properly
options.feedback: If the jaw has not left enough space behind the existing teeth, a wisdom tooth can only partly emerge or come in at an angle.

options.label: They are made of weaker enamel than the other teeth
options.feedback: Wisdom teeth are made of the same enamel as every other tooth; their trouble isn't in what they're made of.

options.label: They grow in before the jaw has finished developing
options.feedback: Wisdom teeth are usually the last teeth to come in, well after the jaw around the other teeth has already settled, not before.

options.label: They are not connected to the jawbone by a root
options.feedback: Wisdom teeth are anchored by roots the same way every other tooth is; what's different about them is only their timing and position.

items.ok_line: Arriving late, into a space that's already full.
items.ko_line: Wisdom teeth are ordinary teeth in every way except one: when and where they try to fit.
items.exp_title: Late arrivals with nowhere to go
items.exp_text: Wisdom teeth are the last molars to develop, typically pushing up at the very back of the jaw well after the rest of the teeth are already in place. If the jaw has not left enough space behind the existing teeth, a wisdom tooth can only partly emerge or come in at an angle, pressing against its neighbour instead of settling in cleanly.

items.prompt: Why does each tooth need its own blood vessels and nerves, hidden inside a structure that looks solid and lifeless from outside?

options.label: To keep the tooth's colour from fading
options.feedback: Blood vessels don't supply pigment to a tooth's visible surface; a tooth's colour comes from the enamel and dentin themselves, not from blood flowing beneath.

options.label: To let the tooth grow larger throughout life
options.feedback: A tooth stops changing size once it has fully formed; blood vessels and nerves inside it are not there to keep it growing.

options.label: To keep the inner living tissue nourished and able to sense damage
options.feedback: The pulp inside every tooth is living tissue, and it needs a blood supply and nerves the same way any other living tissue does.

options.label: To let the tooth repair cracks in its enamel automatically
options.feedback: Enamel has no living cells and cannot repair itself once cracked, no matter how well supplied the tooth's inner tissue is with blood.

items.ok_line: A hard shell wrapped around living tissue.
items.ko_line: Think about what living tissue, as opposed to the hard enamel around it, actually needs to survive.
items.exp_title: A living core inside a hard shell
items.exp_text: Beneath its hard enamel and dentin, every tooth has a soft core called the pulp, threaded with blood vessels that deliver oxygen and nutrients and nerves that can register pressure, heat, or damage. That living core is why a tooth, despite looking like solid, lifeless material from the outside, can ache, and why it needs a blood supply just as any other living tissue does.

items.prompt: Why does a bite work best as a sequence, front teeth first and back teeth last, rather than all teeth doing the same job at once?

options.label: Because the jaw cannot open wide enough to use every tooth at the same time
options.feedback: The jaw opens wide enough to bring every tooth into use during a single bite; the order of use isn't about how far the jaw opens.

options.label: Because each shape of tooth is suited to a different stage of breaking food down
options.feedback: Incisors slice, canines tear, and molars crush and grind, so a bite naturally moves food backward from one shape to the next.

options.label: Because back teeth are weaker and need the front teeth to soften food first
options.feedback: Molars at the back generate more crushing force than the front teeth do, not less, so weakness isn't the reason they come after.

options.label: Because saliva only reaches the front of the mouth at first
options.feedback: Saliva is present throughout the mouth from the start of a bite, not delayed until it reaches further back.

items.ok_line: A different tool for each stage of the job.
items.ko_line: Look at what shape of tooth handles which part of breaking food apart.
items.exp_text: Incisors at the front are shaped to slice off a piece of food, canines just behind them are shaped to tear at anything tougher, and molars further back are shaped to crush and grind what's left into smaller fragments. Because each shape suits a different part of the job, a single bite naturally moves food backward through the mouth from one kind of tooth to the next rather than relying on any one shape to do everything.

items.prompt: Why is saliva important for keeping teeth healthy, beyond simply making food easier to swallow?

options.label: It washes away food debris and helps neutralise acid produced in the mouth
options.feedback: Saliva carries away loose food particles and contains substances that neutralise the acid bacteria produce, keeping enamel from being worn down.

options.label: It hardens enamel further every time the mouth is rinsed with it
options.feedback: Enamel's hardness is fixed once the tooth has formed; saliva does not add further hardness to it over time.

options.label: It carries nutrients directly into the tooth's blood supply
options.feedback: A tooth's blood supply runs through vessels inside the pulp, reached through the root, not through saliva touching the outer surface.

options.label: It seals tiny cracks in the enamel as they form
options.feedback: Enamel has no living cells and cannot be resealed by anything that merely touches its surface, saliva included.

items.ok_line: A rinse and a buffer, both at once.
items.ko_line: Ask what saliva can actually do to something sitting on the tooth's surface, rather than to the tooth's structure itself.
items.exp_text: Saliva flows continuously over the teeth, physically carrying away loose food particles before bacteria can feed on them for long. It also contains substances that neutralise the acid those bacteria produce as they break down leftover sugars, which keeps that acid from sitting against the enamel and wearing it down.
